operations.evidence: BSR's enforcement mission is to protect people and places by regulating building safety and building standards laws in England.
A policy mission does not establish that a particular building or dutyholder is compliant.
A fundamental principle is that those who create risk take responsibility for controlling that risk and complying with the law.
The principle does not by itself identify which person created or controls a specific risk.
BSR uses a range of methods to encourage and support dutyholders to manage risk and comply in a sensible and proportionate way.
Support activity must not be interpreted as approval or immunity from enforcement.
BSR enforcement methods include written information about breaches and verbal warnings.
A warning category does not establish that a warning has been issued in a particular case.
BSR may require improvements in how risks are controlled and managed.
A requirement to improve does not prove that corrective action has been completed or effective.
BSR may require action to remedy non-compliance.
A remedial requirement must not be treated as evidence that the underlying breach is resolved.
BSR may stop activities that create serious risks or do not comply with relevant requirements.
The existence of this power does not establish that a stop notice applies to a named project.
BSR may recommend or bring prosecutions where there has been a serious breach of law.
A prosecution power does not establish guilt, charge, conviction or sentence in any individual case.
BSR may seek appointment of a special measures manager when a person responsible for a higher-risk building fails to carry out building-safety functions.
Appointment requires the applicable legal and tribunal process and cannot be inferred from poor performance alone.
BSR states that enforcement should be firm but fair and proportionate to risk, non-compliance and seriousness of breach.
Proportionality depends on case-specific facts and does not imply uniform outcomes.
BSR targets interventions at buildings and activities with the highest risk, poorly controlled hazards or doubtful safety management.
Risk-based targeting is not a published safety ranking for individual parcels or buildings.
Where several dutyholders have responsibilities, BSR may target enforcement against more than one when appropriate.
Multiple possible dutyholders must not be converted into shared liability without legal and factual analysis.
When non-compliance is identified, regulators should explain the decision, reasons, required actions, reasonable timescales and consequences of non-compliance.
An explanation or agreed timescale is not evidence that compliance has been achieved.
For higher-risk building work, BSR can use compliance notices and stop notices in the circumstances described by the policy.
Notice powers must not be treated as proof that a particular notice has been served or remains in force.
For occupied higher-risk buildings, a compliance notice may require an accountable person to act within a period and may be urgent where people face imminent danger.
An urgent-action power does not establish imminent danger at a specific building without regulator evidence.
The revised 2025 guidance clarifies that regulation 10 is not intended to require existing flat entrance doors to meet current new-build door standards.
The clarification does not excuse inadequate doors or defects identified by a fire-risk assessment.
A door that met the relevant standard when the block or door was built may remain adequate if it is undamaged and gaps are not excessive.
Age or original compliance alone does not prove present adequacy.
Absence of certification, intumescent strips or smoke seals does not by itself mean an existing door is unfit for purpose.
Their absence must still be considered with the fire-risk assessment, door design and condition.
Regulation 10 applies to blocks containing at least two domestic premises and common parts used for evacuation, including purpose-built and converted blocks.
The rule does not establish whether a named property meets the statutory premises definition.
The responsible person for communal parts is responsible for arranging the checks required by the regulations.
The guidance does not identify the responsible person for a specific ownership or management structure.
Information about flat entrance doors must be provided to residents in all blocks within regulation 10's scope.
Providing information is not evidence that doors have been inspected or repaired.
Routine regulation 10 checks apply where the building's top storey is more than 11 metres above ground level.
Height and storey status require building-specific measurement.
A suitable and sufficient fire-risk assessment should identify relevant doors and assess whether they adequately resist fire and smoke.
A fire-risk assessment record does not prove that its findings remain current or implemented.
Where a door is inadequate or needs repair or replacement, the work must be undertaken by a competent person or contractor.
A contractor's appointment or certificate does not prove that every defect was properly corrected.
Residents must be told to keep fire doors shut, not tamper with self-closing devices and report faults or damage immediately.
Resident information does not establish actual resident behaviour or door condition.
Fire-door information must be provided to new residents as soon as reasonably practicable and repeated at intervals not exceeding 12 months.
A distribution schedule does not prove that every resident received or understood the information.
For buildings above the threshold, flat entrance doors require best-endeavours checks at least annually and communal fire doors at least every three months.
Frequency compliance does not establish the adequacy or quality of each check.
Regulation 10 checks are intended to be simple visual checks that generally do not require tools or a specialist.
Simple checks do not replace specialist assessment within the wider fire-risk-assessment process.
Responsible persons should arrange access with residents and record steps taken, including cases where access was not granted.
Recorded attempts do not prove that a door was inspected or that legal action is justified.
Checks should cover damage, glazing, hinges, seals where present, excessive gaps and effective full self-closing from different opening angles.
A visual pass does not establish certified fire resistance or future performance during a fire.
